transcript.text: Can you describe your key responsibilities as Plant Head where you run a plant of about 200 people with 5 functional heads reporting to you?

I have twelve years in manufacturing and have been the plant head of an auto-components plant for the last six. About 200 people work there, and five functional heads report to me. My main work in the last two years was raising line efficiency from 71% to 82%, mostly through line-balancing and preventive maintenance. I'm applying for an executive MBA because I run the plant well but have no training in finance, pricing or strategy, which is what the next role needs.
What specific strategies did you implement to improve line efficiency from 71% to 82%?
transcript.anchor_quote: raising line efficiency from 71% to 82%, mostly through line-balancing and preventive maintenance

transcript.text: On line-balancing, I went through the longest-cycle station first and we found that two operators were waiting for material. We moved the supply point and added a kanban card. That alone gave us about three points of efficiency.
How did you manage the challenges involved in line-balancing and what metrics did you track to measure preventive maintenance effectiveness?
transcript.anchor_quote: we found that two operators were waiting for material. We moved the supply point and added a kanban card

transcript.text: I believe in empowering my people and creating a culture of ownership and excellence. We follow a continuous-improvement mindset across the shop floor, and that drives the numbers.
Can you provide an example of a situation where empowering your team and fostering a culture of ownership led to a significant improvement or problem resolution at the plant?
The rejections fell from 1,800 ppm to 900 ppm in my first month as plant head. Honestly it was an easy gain and it took very little effort.
What specific actions did you take to achieve the reduction in customer rejections from 1,800 ppm to 900 ppm, and how did you sustain this improvement?
transcript.anchor_quote: The rejections fell from 1,800 ppm to 900 ppm in my first month as plant head

transcript.text: I don't know the exact share of our rejections caused by the supplier's castings. The quality head tracks that, and I haven't looked at it recently.
How do you allocate responsibility between yourself and your functional heads when addressing quality issues like customer rejections?
transcript.anchor_quote: I haven't looked at it recently

transcript.text: I don't accept that a plant head only manages machines. Most of my day goes into people and customers. I'd ask you to reconsider the question, because I'm not an operations-only person.
Tell me about a decision where the trade-offs were not obvious. How did you decide?
I can't say our monthly volumes or which OEMs we supply. Those are covered by customer agreements, and I'd get into trouble.
How do you balance the trade-offs between operational efficiency, product quality, and employee engagement in your decisions as a plant head?
transcript.anchor_quote: I don't accept that a plant head only manages machines. Most of my day goes into people and customers

transcript.text: I think I've answered enough for today. Could we end the practice session here? I'd like to read the feedback.

feedback.summary: The candidate demonstrates clear ownership and scope as a plant head, notably raising line efficiency and reducing customer rejections with specific, impactful actions. They emphasize people management and culture, reflecting a balanced leadership approach aligned with their general management ambitions. However, there were limited elaborations on trade-offs and quantitative outcomes for preventive maintenance, and some hesitation to engage on quality metrics or decision trade-offs constrained the evidence of judgment and learning from setbacks. The candidate also declined to discuss some specifics due to confidentiality, which is respected but limits assessment on business insights and peer contribution.
